title: MA9-10477
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX, a citizen of Ukraine, is claiming refugee protection under section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (the Act). The panel has taken into account the IRB Chairperson's guidelines on Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution.

The claimant alleged that in XXXX 2008, she began a romantic relationship with XXXX XXXX, the general manager of the XXXX for which she worked. On Friday, XXXX XXXX XXXX 2008, he visited her at her home and told her that auditors had come to the XXXX and suspected XXXX. A XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. Since the claimant XXXX XXXX XXXX, he asked her to sign some papers and arranged it so that liability for this transaction fell on the shoulders of the regional director, Mr. XXXX. The claimant, who was told a few days before by Mr. XXXX to be wary of XXXX because he had ties with organized crime, refused to sign these papers and told him that she was suspicious of his ties with these people. Angered, XXXX slapped and insulted her. The claimant then asked him to leave her home.

On Monday, XXXX XXXX XXXX 2008, the claimant was heading to work when she was stopped by a car. A man got out of the car and told her to go to work and to be quiet. He also told her to do everything XXXX told her to do and that if she did anything to the contrary, he would not kill her but would disfigure her. The claimant noted the car's licence plate number. She went to the police to report these threats. The officer in charge listened to her, took a few notes and asked her to wait. Fifteen minutes later, the detective invited her into his office and asked her if she had noted the licence plate number, because the owner of the car did not match the description of the man that she gave. Also, the owner of the car told them on the telephone that no one except him could have driven this vehicle. Confused, the claimant went to work. At the end of the day, XXXX came to apologize for the way he behaved on Friday night. He invited her to a restaurant. At about 10:00 p.m., the waiter came to tell XXXX that someone sitting farther in the restaurant wanted to speak with him. XXXX went to see this person, and he returned distraught. He told the claimant that this man was the owner of all the XXXX XXXX in the district, as well as XXXX XXXX. It was to him that the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. He asked him to remove his name from the list of XXXX, or else he and she would have major problems. This man walked by their table and let them know that their lives were not worth very much. The claimant offered to go to the police with XXXX, but he said that the police would never go after this important man.

A week later, the director of the XXXX XXXX, Mr. XXXX, was killed in a car accident. The claimant believes that these people killed him. When she found out about this, she went to XXXX's home; he calmed her down and told her that everything had been resolved. He offered her tickets so that she could go and relax in Budapest. She went there alone from XXXX XXXX to XXXX XXXX, 2008. When she returned, she found out that she had lost her job. She heard nothing more from XXXX, and he did not show up for work. The claimant decided to write a letter to the prosecutor in which she discussed XXXXs disappearance and its possible connection to the mafia. She also recounted the strange car accident in which Mr. XXXX was killed. She stated that she did not receive a response. Two weeks later, she telephoned them, and she was told that her letter had probably been forwarded to XXXX regional department of internal affairs. From there, she was told that the letter had been sent to the XXXX police for investigation and that she should approach them. On XXXX XXXX, 2008, she went to these offices and was rudely told that she was not allowed to know what was happening with this investigation. When she told them that she suspected that her boyfriend XXXX and his former director had been killed, she was told to return in two days to see the investigator. Two days later, when she was headed toward the police station, she was kidnapped and taken to a house, where she stayed for three days. She was told that she had to provide them with documents regarding the XXXX XXXX. She was asked about XXXX whereabouts. She was beaten and raped. The metal screen in the bathroom was attached from the inside with screws. She managed to remove it, and she escaped. She took refuge at her cousin's home and stayed there until she left for Canada in XXXX 2009.
The panel determines that the claimant is not a "Convention refugee" or a "person in need of protection" for the following reasons.

The panel cannot establish a nexus between the fear of persecution raised by the claimant and one of the five grounds set out in section 96 of the Act. Accordingly, the panel will conduct its analysis under subsection 97(1) of the Act. Identity

The claimant's identity has been established to the panel's satisfaction by means of a copy of her passport, which was issued by the Ukrainian authorities and filed as evidence by Immigration services.1 Credibility

The claimant stated that she went to take refuge at her cousin's home after she escaped, around XXXX XXXX XXXX 2008. Only in XXXX 2009 did the claimant apply for a Canadian visa. When asked to explain why she waited so long-until XXXX 2009-to apply for a visa, the claimant testified that her father had filed this application for her and that he first tried for Europe. When he realized that this would not work, he asked the claimant's sister, who lives in Canada, to send him an invitation. The panel does not accept this explanation because the time between when the claimant alleged that her life was at risk (and therefore had to hide) and the time when her father filed the visa application was very long. It is reasonable to believe that if the claimant's life was really at risk, her father would not have waited so long before asking his daughter in Canada to send him an invitation for her sister, who was in danger. Even if he had explored other options, like Europe, it is reasonable to believe that he would not have waited so long before realizing that this would not work. Furthermore, why would he not have started by the visa application in Canada since the claimant's sister has been in Canada for several years, having been accepted as a refugee?2 This undermines the claimant's subjective fear.

The claimant stated that she fears organized crime in her city and specifically XXXX XXXX, who apparently led this organization. She allegedly met him briefly one time in a restaurant on Monday, XXXX XXXX XXXX 2008, when she was at this restaurant with her lover, XXXX. The claimant was confronted with the fact that this date had been amended3 in the narrative of her Personal Information Form (PIF)4 as being XXXX XXXX, 2008, instead. This information had also been discussed at the start of the hearing because the panel had not received this amendment. When asked to explain why she stated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2008, the claimant answered that she was mistaken when she stated XXXX XXXX because it had been written that way before in the form. This response leaves the panel confused because this information was discussed a few minutes earlier. It is reasonable to believe that the claimant knew that the date was not the right one because it had been changed. This undermines the claimant's credibility.

The claimant believes that her boss, Mr. XXXX, who allegedly died in a car accident, was a victim of the mafia because of the fraud discovered by the auditors at the bank. She stated that he died on the Saturday of the week following the Monday that she and XXXX went to dinner at the restaurant. Since that Monday was XXXX XXXX XXXX 2008, it was either XXXX XXXX or XXXX, 2008. The claimant then stated that it must have been XXXX XXXX XXXX 2008. When confronted with the evidence that she submitted under P-9,5 which indicates that the accident allegedly happened on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2008, the claimant stated that she did not know whether it was Saturday or Sunday, but that it was definitely that weekend.

The claimant submitted a newspaper excerpt6 in which the employees of the bank allegedly sent a condolence message to the director's family following his death. The claimant does not have the original newspaper; she stated that her father had sent it to her and that he did not send the original. She believes that it was perhaps because he found this article at the archives. The panel does not accept this explanation and draws a negative inference from the fact that the claimant did not produce the original newspaper, which prevents the panel from verifying its genuineness.

The date of this newspaper excerpt was not translated in the official translation provided by the claimant7 before the hearing. The panel therefore asked the Russian interpreter in the room to translate the date. However, the interpreter informed the panel that the information on this document was not in Russian and seemed to be in Ukrainian, so he could not translate the date. The panel therefore requested that this date be translated and gave a deadline to have this done. The panel received the requested translation and listed this document as P-16. It is indicated that the date of this newspaper is XXXX XXXX XXXX 2008. How could people have issued condolences in a newspaper dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2008, if the person died only on XXXX XXXX, 2008? The claimant submitted, along with the new translation, a written explanation stating that this newspaper is published only once a week and that the publication in question covered the period from XXXX XXXX to XXXX XXXX 2008. The panel does not accept this explanation and finds that the claimant is attempting to find a response to this striking implausibility. It is reasonable to believe that if a newspaper covers a period of several days, it would be indicated, or the publication date would be the last day covered in the period and not the first. The panel is of the opinion that this document is not genuine. Therefore, it attaches no probative value to this document.8 This undermines the claimant's credibility and leads the panel to doubt her story.

The claimant stated that when she returned from Budapest on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2008, she found out that she no longer had a job. She stated that she was kidnapped on XXXX XXXX, 2008, and that she was detained for three days before she managed to escape. The panel asked her what these people wanted from her and why they had kidnapped her. The claimant answered that they wanted her to return the loan documents to them. The panel asked her if they had talked about anything else. The claimant repeated that they wanted the documents. The panel confronted her with her narrative, in which she indicated that they had asked her about XXXX's whereabouts. When asked to explain this omission in her testimony, the claimant stated that they had asked her this but that on the whole, it was all about the documents. The panel does not accept this explanation and is of the opinion that the claimant is attempting to adjust her testimony with respect to the omission before her. The panel is of the opinion that if she had been kidnapped and questioned about her lover XXXX, it would have made her distressed. Also, the claimant stated that she thought that these people had killed XXXX. If these people had asked her XXXX's whereabouts, why would she say they had killed him? All of this is inconsistent, because if they had killed him, it would be reasonable to believe that they would not have asked her his whereabouts.

The claimant was asked for the documents pertaining to this monetary transaction. The panel asked her why these people would have asked her for documents from the bank regarding this transaction given that she no longer worked there. The claimant stated that she did not know? perhaps because she was still in a relationship with XXXX. The panel does not accept this explanation. All of this is inconsistent, and the panel does not believe that the claimant was kidnapped or detained.

The claimant stated that these people are still searching for her. The panel asked her whether these people had harassed her parents, who were still in Ukraine. The claimant stated no. The panel does not believe that these people would still be searching for the claimant without looking for her at parents' home, particularly since she testified that their address is still her official address.

For all these reasons, the panel does not believe the claimant's story that she is being sought by organized crime associates. For these reasons, the panel attaches no probative value to documents P-8 and P-9, which are supposedly responses from the department of internal affairs. It also attaches no probative value to P-10 through P-12, which are supposedly medical certificates. Furthermore, the documentary evidence9 indicates that "it is possible to obtain fraudulent medical and police reports throughout Ukraine" because "police officials and hospital staff in Ukraine earn a low salary and some are therefore willing to accept money to produce such fraudulent documents." The panel has already found that the document submitted by the claimant under P-13 was not a genuine document.

After analyzing all of the testimonial and documentary evidence, the panel is of the opinion that the claimant's testimony is not credible and that she did not discharge her burden of establishing that there is a serious possibility of her being persecuted on a Convention ground if she returned to Ukraine. She was also not successful in demonstrating, on a balance of probabilities, that in returning to Ukraine, she would be personally subjected to a danger of torture, to a risk to her life, or to a risk of a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment.

For all of these reasons, the panel therefore determines that XXXX XXXX is not a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. Consequently, the panel rejects her claim for refugee protection.
